title: Be om gjentakelse eller forklaring — ask for repetition or clarification
goal: Identify the communication problem, choose a repair move, confirm the corrected message, and continue.

objectives.statement: Identify the communication problem, choose a repair move, confirm the corrected message, and continue.

sections.title: A message that does not arrive clearly

spans.value: Mina has recently started helping at a small community café in Bergen. During her first morning shift, her colleague Jonas explains where an order should go. The room is noisy, and Mina misses part of the message.
Mina, kan du sette kaffen på bordet ved vinduet?

blocks.translation: Jonas: Mina, can you put the coffee on the table by the window?

spans.value: Unnskyld, kan du gjenta?

blocks.translation: Mina: Sorry, can you repeat that?

spans.value: Kan du sette kaffen på bordet ved vinduet?

blocks.translation: Jonas: Can you put the coffee on the table by the window?

spans.value: Mina hears the sentence this time, but she is not sure which table Jonas means.
Mener du det lille bordet?

blocks.translation: Mina: Do you mean the small table?

spans.value: Ja, det lille bordet ved vinduet.

blocks.translation: Jonas: Yes, the small table by the window.

spans.value: Å ja, det lille bordet. Greit!

blocks.translation: Mina: Oh yes, the small table. All right!

spans.value: Mina then takes the coffee to the correct table.

This short exchange contains a complete communication repair. Mina first notices the problem: she did not hear the message. She asks Jonas to repeat it. After hearing it again, she identifies a second, more specific problem: she does not know which table he means. She checks the detail, confirms the corrected message, and continues with the task.
That sequence is the focus of this chapter:
You do not need to understand every Norwegian word immediately. You need a way to keep the conversation moving when understanding breaks down.

sections.title: First repair move: ask for repetition

spans.value: When you do not hear a message, ask the speaker to say it again.
This is polite, clear, and useful in many situations.
Unnskyld
can attract attention or soften the request. The central request is:
You can also say:

no.value: Kan du si det en gang til?

en.value: Can you say that one more time?

spans.value: Both requests concern the whole message. They are useful when noise, speed, distance, or unfamiliar pronunciation prevents you from hearing enough.
At the café, Mina could use either form:

no.value: Unnskyld, kan du si det en gang til?

en.value: Sorry, can you say that one more time?

spans.value: The speaker will normally understand that repetition is needed. A brief
Hva?
What?
—may sometimes be heard in casual conversation, but it can sound abrupt. At A1 level,
Unnskyld, kan du gjenta?
is a safer general-purpose choice.

Read or listen to a short café exchange in which Jonas gives Mina an instruction, but surrounding noise hides part of it. Decide whether Mina should ask for repetition or ask about one particular word. Then formulate a polite repair request.

This activity belongs here because the first decision is not which phrase you remember; it is what kind of communication problem has occurred. The café context continues the opening situation. A successful response would show that you recognize a missing whole message and use a request such as
Kan du gjenta?
Can you repeat that?
—rather than pretending to understand.

sections.title: When repetition is not enough: ask for slower speech

spans.value: Sometimes you can hear the speaker, but the message arrives too quickly. Repeating it at the same speed may not solve the problem. Ask the person to speak more slowly.

en.value: Can you speak a little more slowly?

spans.value: The word
litt
a little
—makes the request sound natural and moderate.
Takk
thank you/please
—adds politeness.
Imagine that Jonas gives Mina several details quickly:
Kunden vil ha to kaffe, ett glass vann og en bolle.

blocks.translation: Jonas: The customer wants two coffees, one glass of water, and a bun.

spans.value: Mina hears the words, but not clearly enough to follow the full order.
Kan du snakke litt saktere?

blocks.translation: Mina: Can you speak a little more slowly?

spans.value: Ja. To kaffe, ett glass vann og en bolle.

blocks.translation: Jonas: Yes. Two coffees, one glass of water, and a bun.

spans.value: To kaffe, ett glass vann og en bolle. Greit.

blocks.translation: Mina: Two coffees, one glass of water, and a bun. All right.

spans.value: Here Mina does more than say that she has understood. She repeats the important information. This gives Jonas an opportunity to correct her if necessary.
Compare the two repair moves:
Use this when you did not hear the message or missed a large part of it.

en.value: Can you speak a little more slowly?

spans.value: Use this when speed is the main problem.
In real conversation, both problems can occur together. You can combine the requests:

en.value: Can you repeat that a little more slowly?

spans.value: This compact request tells the speaker exactly what would help.

sections.title: Checkpoint: choosing help that matches the problem

spans.value: Work with three brief situations: a noisy room, a speaker who talks too quickly, and a message that disappears because you were looking away. For each situation, state the communication problem and make one suitable request in Norwegian.

This activity belongs here because effective repair depends on matching the request to the obstacle. Use everyday contexts such as the café counter, a bus stop, or a short telephone call. A successful response would demonstrate that you can distinguish a need for repetition from a need for slower speech and choose a clear, polite request.
You may hear most of a sentence but fail to understand one word or expression. In that case, asking for the entire message again may be unnecessary. Point to the unclear part.
These questions solve slightly different problems.
Use
Hva betyr …?
What does … mean?
—when a word or expression is unfamiliar.

en.value: “Ledig” means that nobody is using the table.

spans.value: Use
Hva mener du?
What do you mean?
—when you heard the words but do not understand the speaker’s intended message.
Du kan ta den etterpå.

blocks.translation: Jonas: You can take it afterwards.

spans.value: Unnskyld, hva mener du?

blocks.translation: Mina: Sorry, what do you mean?

spans.value: Du kan ta pause etter at kundene går.

blocks.translation: Jonas: You can take a break after the customers leave.

spans.value: Å, pause etterpå. Nå forstår jeg.

blocks.translation: Mina: Oh, a break afterwards. Now I understand.

spans.value: Mina does not merely request help. After Jonas explains, she states the corrected interpretation:
pause etterpå
a break afterwards
. She then confirms that communication can continue:
Nå forstår jeg
Now I understand.
A useful short pattern is:
The final line matters. It closes the repair sequence and tells the other person that no further explanation is needed.

Return to Mina’s shift. Jonas uses one unfamiliar word in an otherwise understandable instruction. Ask what that word means. After receiving a simple explanation, confirm the meaning in your own short response and indicate that you now understand.

This activity belongs here because learners often understand enough to identify one specific gap. Asking about that gap is more efficient than restarting the whole conversation. A successful response would contain a focused question such as
Hva betyr …?
What does … mean?
—followed by a confirmation such as
Å, nå forstår jeg
Oh, now I understand.

sections.title: Check a detail with Mener du …?

spans.value: Sometimes every word is familiar, but one detail remains uncertain. Mina heard
bordet ved vinduet
the table by the window
—but there was more than one possible table. She checked her interpretation:

en.value: Do you mean the small table?

spans.value: Mener du …?
Do you mean …?
—allows you to offer your best interpretation and ask the speaker to confirm or correct it.

en.value: Do you mean at two o’clock?
Do you mean the bus to the city centre?

spans.value: This move is especially useful for places, times, people, numbers, and objects.
A repair can be very short:
Vi møtes utenfor.

blocks.translation: Aksel: We’ll meet outside.

spans.value: Mener du utenfor biblioteket?

blocks.translation: Nora: Do you mean outside the library?

spans.value: Ja, utenfor biblioteket.

blocks.translation: Aksel: Yes, outside the library.

spans.value: Fint, vi ses der.

blocks.translation: Nora: Good, see you there.

spans.value: Nora identifies the uncertain detail, proposes an interpretation, receives confirmation, and continues by accepting the arrangement.
If the interpretation is wrong, the other person corrects it:
Vi møtes utenfor.

blocks.translation: Aksel: We’ll meet outside.

spans.value: Mener du utenfor biblioteket?

blocks.translation: Nora: Do you mean outside the library?

spans.value: Nei, utenfor kinoen.

blocks.translation: Aksel: No, outside the cinema.

spans.value: Å, utenfor kinoen. Vi ses der.

blocks.translation: Nora: Oh, outside the cinema. See you there.

spans.value: Notice how Nora repeats the corrected place. A simple
Ja
Yes
—would not show whether she had registered the correction.
Å, utenfor kinoen
Oh, outside the cinema
—makes the repaired message explicit.

sections.title: Checkpoint: confirming a place, time, or object

spans.value: Use short situations in which most of the message is clear but one detail could have two interpretations. Ask
Mener du …?
Do you mean …?
—with your best interpretation. Then respond to either confirmation or correction by repeating the final detail and continuing the exchange.

This activity belongs here because partial understanding calls for a focused check, not a general request for repetition. Use familiar details from the café and other everyday settings: which table, which drink, which stop, or what time. A successful response would demonstrate that you can test an interpretation, accept a correction, and continue with the corrected information.
After the speaker repeats or explains, do not leave the exchange unfinished. Confirm what you now understand.
Several short confirmation expressions are useful:
Repeating the crucial information is often stronger than saying only
Jeg forstår
I understand
Compare:
This signals acceptance, but it does not reveal what you understood.

no.value: Greit, to kaffe og ett glass vann.

en.value: All right, two coffees and one glass of water.

spans.value: This confirms the important details and lets the speaker detect an error.
A useful full sequence is:

no.value: To kaffe og ett glass vann.

en.value: Two coffees and one glass of water.

no.value: Å ja, to kaffe og ett glass vann. Greit.

en.value: Oh yes, two coffees and one glass of water. All right.

spans.value: Another sequence begins with a specific check:

en.value: Do you mean the table by the door?
No, the table by the window.

no.value: Å, bordet ved vinduet. Jeg tar kaffen dit.

en.value: Oh, the table by the window. I’ll take the coffee there.

spans.value: The final sentence continues the task. Communication repair is not complete until both people can move on.

Take a short interrupted exchange and supply Mina’s contributions at three stages: request help, confirm the corrected message, and continue with the café task. The initial problem might be a missed order, an unfamiliar word, or uncertainty about a table.

This activity belongs here because knowing one repair phrase is not the full outcome. The learner must carry the exchange from breakdown to successful continuation. A successful response would match the repair move to the problem, repeat or acknowledge the corrected information, and add a natural next step such as
Greit, jeg gjør det nå
All right, I’ll do it now.
A learner may say
Ja
Yes
—even when the message is unclear. This keeps the conversation moving for a moment, but often creates a larger problem later.
If you do not hear an order, say:
Do not confirm information that you have not understood.

sections.title: Using a general question for a specific problem

spans.value: If only one word is unfamiliar,
Kan du gjenta?
Can you repeat that?
—may produce exactly the same unfamiliar word. Ask directly:
If only the location is uncertain, check it:

en.value: Do you mean the table by the door?

spans.value: A specific repair request makes a useful answer more likely.

sections.title: Asking for slower speech when meaning is the problem

spans.value: Kan du snakke litt saktere?
Can you speak a little more slowly?
—helps when speed prevents understanding. It does not explain an unknown word. If the word itself is the obstacle, use
Hva betyr …?
What does … mean?
Consider this exchange:
Nei, jeg mener bord fem.

blocks.translation: Jonas: No, I mean table five.

spans.value: Greit.

blocks.translation: Mina: All right.

spans.value: Mina may have understood, but Jonas cannot be certain. A clearer response is:
Repeating the corrected detail shows that the repair worked.
After an explanation, add a brief confirmation and next step:

no.value: Å ja, nå forstår jeg. Jeg tar den med en gang.

en.value: Oh yes, now I understand. I’ll take it right away.

spans.value: This sounds more complete than asking a question and then giving no response.
Later in the morning, Jonas gives Mina another message.
Mina, kunden ved døra vil betale med kort, og etterpå kan du rydde bord seks.

blocks.translation: Jonas: Mina, the customer by the door wants to pay by card, and afterwards you can clear table six.

spans.value: Mina hears most of the message, but Jonas speaks too quickly.
Unnskyld, kan du gjenta litt saktere?

blocks.translation: Mina: Sorry, can you repeat that a little more slowly?

spans.value: Kunden ved døra vil betale med kort. Etterpå kan du rydde bord seks.

blocks.translation: Jonas: The customer by the door wants to pay by card. Afterwards you can clear table six.

spans.value: Mina is unsure about the table number.
Mener du bord seksten?

blocks.translation: Mina: Do you mean table sixteen?

spans.value: Nei, bord seks.

blocks.translation: Jonas: No, table six.

spans.value: Å, bord seks. Først hjelper jeg kunden, og så rydder jeg bordet.

blocks.translation: Mina: Oh, table six. First I’ll help the customer, and then I’ll clear the table.

spans.value: This time Mina handles the complete repair independently. She identifies speed as the first problem and requests slower repetition. She then identifies one uncertain detail and checks it. Jonas corrects the number. Mina repeats the corrected number and states what she will do next.

sections.title: Integrated practice: repairing a complete exchange

spans.value: Create a guided exchange based on Mina’s workday. Begin with a message that contains one realistic communication problem: Mina misses the whole message, the speaker is too fast, one word is unfamiliar, or one detail is uncertain. Have Mina choose a matching repair move. After the message is repeated, explained, or corrected, have her confirm the important information and continue the task.

This activity belongs near the end because it combines all stages without changing the lesson’s communicative goal. The context remains concrete and familiar. A successful response would make the problem visible through the chosen request, show that Mina has understood the corrected message, and end with a relevant continuation rather than stopping after the repair phrase.

Without looking back, produce one Norwegian request for each of these situations: you did not hear the message, the speaker is too fast, one word is unfamiliar, and one detail may be wrong. Then choose one situation and complete the full sequence: identify the problem, request help, confirm the corrected message, and continue.
A successful review response would use an appropriate repair move, clearly acknowledge the final information, and return naturally to the conversation or task.

prompt.value: In a noisy café exchange, Jonas gives Mina an instruction, but surrounding noise hides the whole message. Choose the complete interpretation and polite repair request.

options.text: Jeg fikk ikke med meg hele beskjeden. «Kan du gjenta?» — Can you repeat that?
options.why: The whole message was missed, so a repetition request is appropriate.

options.text: Jeg forstår resten, men ett ord er uklart. «Hva betyr …?» — What does … mean?
options.why: This asks about one word, but the problem is a missing whole message.

stem.value: Choose the response that identifies the communication problem and uses the appropriate repair.

prompt.value: Mina faces three situations: a noisy room, a speaker who talks too quickly, and a message she missed because she was looking away. Choose the complete set that names each problem and matches it with a clear, polite Norwegian request.

options.text: 1. Det er bråk, men jeg spør «Hva betyr …?» — What does … mean? 2. Taleren snakker for fort, så jeg spør «Kan du gjenta?» — Can you repeat that? 3. Jeg så bort, men jeg spør «Mener du …?» — Do you mean …?
options.why: The set uses a word-meaning question or interpretation check where repetition or slower speech is needed.

options.text: 1. Det er bråk, så jeg hørte ikke hele beskjeden. «Kan du gjenta?» — Can you repeat that? 2. Taleren snakker for fort. «Kan du snakke saktere?» — Can you speak more slowly? 3. Jeg så bort og fikk ikke med meg beskjeden. «Kan du gjenta?» — Can you repeat that?
options.why: Each request matches the specific communication obstacle.

stem.value: Which complete set matches all three communication obstacles with suitable requests?

prompt.value: Jonas tells Mina: «Ta koppen til bord 3.» Mina understands the instruction except for the word koppen. Jonas then explains: «Koppen er en liten drikkebeholder med hank.» Write Mina’s two short Norwegian contributions: first ask what koppen means; after this explanation, confirm in Norwegian that koppen is a small drinking container with a handle and show that she now understands.

payload.judge_prompt: Check for both stages. Accept natural Bokmål variants of «Hva betyr …?» (What does … mean?) for the focused question. After an explanation, require a Norwegian confirmation of the explained meaning and an indication that Mina now understands, such as «Å, nå forstår jeg» (Oh, now I understand).

criteria.instruction: Asks what the unfamiliar word means with a focused Norwegian question.
Confirms in Norwegian that koppen is a small drinking container with a handle after receiving the explanation.
Indicates in Norwegian that Mina now understands.

prompt.value: At a bus stop, Jonas says: «Ta vesken til plattform 3.» Mina is unsure whether he means platform 2 or platform 3. Write Mina’s two short Norwegian contributions: ask «Mener du …?» — Do you mean …? with her best interpretation; then use one of these supplied replies from Jonas — «Ja, plattform 3.» or «Nei, plattform 2.» — and repeat the final platform and continue the task.

payload.judge_prompt: Accept either a confirmation or correction branch. Require the first contribution to ask a focused Norwegian «Mener du …?» (Do you mean …?) question about one ambiguous detail. Require the second contribution to repeat the confirmed or corrected final detail and continue the task. Accept natural Bokmål variants.

criteria.instruction: Uses a focused Norwegian check with Mener du …? about one ambiguous detail.
Repeats the confirmed or corrected final place, time, or object in Norwegian.
Continues the exchange with a relevant next step based on the final detail.

prompt.value: At the café, Jonas tells Mina to bring two cups of coffee to table 4, but she misses the whole order. Write Mina’s three short Norwegian contributions: request repetition; after Jonas repeats «Ta to kopper kaffe til bord 4.», confirm the order; and continue with the café task.

payload.judge_prompt: Check the three-stage repair cycle. Accept natural Bokmål variants, including «Kan du gjenta?» (Can you repeat that?) for the missed whole order, a confirmation that repeats or clearly acknowledges two cups of coffee for table 4, and a relevant continuation such as «Greit, jeg gjør det nå» (All right, I’ll do it now).

criteria.instruction: Uses a repetition request because Mina missed the whole café order.
Repeats or acknowledges the complete repeated order in Norwegian.
Adds a natural Norwegian next step for the café task.

prompt.value: Choose one of these four everyday situations and write three short Norwegian contributions: (1) Jonas says «Ta to kopper kaffe til bord 4.», but noise hides the whole message; after Mina asks for repetition, Jonas repeats that sentence. (2) Jonas says «Sett kaken på bord 2.» too quickly; after Mina asks him to speak more slowly, he repeats that sentence. (3) Jonas says «Ta koppen til bord 3.» and koppen is unfamiliar; after Mina asks what it means, Jonas explains «Koppen er en liten drikkebeholder med hank.» (4) Jonas says «Ta vesken til plattform 3.» and Mina is unsure whether he means platform 2 or 3; after Mina asks «Mener du …?», Jonas replies «Ja, plattform 3.» or «Nei, plattform 2.». Use the matching taught move: «Kan du gjenta?» — Can you repeat that?; «Kan du snakke saktere?» — Can you speak more slowly?; «Hva betyr …?» — What does … mean?; or «Mener du …?» — Do you mean …?. After the supplied repair reply, confirm the important information and continue the selected situation. Make the selected problem visible through the request and end with a relevant next step.

payload.judge_prompt: Accept one of the four routes only when the Norwegian repair request matches the selected problem: «Kan du gjenta?» (Can you repeat that?) for a missed message, «Kan du snakke saktere?» (Can you speak more slowly?) for speech that is too fast, «Hva betyr …?» (What does … mean?) for an unfamiliar word, or «Mener du …?» (Do you mean …?) for an uncertain detail. Require a confirmation or acknowledgment of the important information after repair and a relevant continuation in the selected situation. The response must not stop after the repair request.

criteria.instruction: Makes one selected communication problem visible through the matching Norwegian repair request.
Confirms or acknowledges the important corrected information in Norwegian after repair.
Ends with a relevant Norwegian continuation of the selected situation.

prompt.value: Write one natural Norwegian request for each situation: you did not hear the message; the speaker is too fast; one word is unfamiliar; or one detail may be wrong. Then choose one situation and write a complete Norwegian repair sequence: briefly identify the problem, request help, acknowledge the corrected message, and return naturally to the conversation or task. Use a new everyday context such as a bus stop or short telephone call.

payload.judge_prompt: Check all four retrieval items and one complete sequence. Accept natural Bokmål variants, but require the canonical meanings «Kan du gjenta?» (Can you repeat that?) for a missed message, «Kan du snakke saktere?» (Can you speak more slowly?) for speech that is too fast, «Hva betyr …?» (What does … mean?) for an unfamiliar word, and «Mener du …?» (Do you mean …?) for an uncertain detail. In the selected sequence, require a matching request, a clear Norwegian acknowledgment or repetition of the final information, and a natural continuation such as «Å, nå forstår jeg» (Oh, now I understand) and «Greit, jeg gjør det nå» (All right, I’ll do it now).

criteria.instruction: Provides one distinct Norwegian request for each listed communication problem, with every request matched to its problem.
Identifies one chosen problem and uses the matching repair request in a complete sequence.
Clearly acknowledges or repeats the final information in Norwegian.
Returns naturally to the conversation or task in Norwegian.
